A mixture of freezing rain sleet and snow changed over to all snow during the early morning hours of February 17th. The Cooperative Observer 3 miles northwest of Cole Camp reported 1.8 inches of  sleet and snow, while the CoCoRaHs station MO-BT-11 3.8 miles north northeast of Warsaw reported 1.2 inches of sleet, freezing rain, and snow. A public report of a measured 3.0 inches of sleet and snow was received 1 mile east southeast of Warsaw. Roads were snow and ice covered and hazardous. MODOT reported that the freezing rain along with the sleet and snow made the roads a big chunk of ice. There were numerous side-offs and schools were closed for the day.

There were 2 rounds of wintry precipitation that fell across the county. Rain changed to a mix of freezing rain, sleet, and snow during the early morning hours of February 2, then changed to all snow before ending around midday. There were 3 rounds of wintry precipitation that fell across the county. Rain changed to a mix of freezing rain, sleet, and snow during the early morning hours of February 2, then changed to all snow before ending around midday. There was a lull in the action before another round of just snow began early that evening and continued into the day February 3. The ASOS in Joplin reported 0.11 inches of flat ice accumulation with the initial round, with other reports of 1 to 2 inches of sleet and snow.  The third round of snow began the evening of February 3 and ending during the early morning hours of February 4. Additional snow amounts with the second and third rounds resulted in total snow accumulations of 4 to 6 inches, with the higher amounts across the eastern sections of the county. The CoCoRaHS station 4.5 miles east of Carthage reported a total sleet and snow accumulation of 4.5 inches. A Carthage special Road District snow plow slid off the road and overturned the morning of February 3. Schools were closed across the county through the period.

Rain changed to sleet and snow just after midnight February 2 and ended late in the afternoon. After a brief lull, snow began to fall once again late in the evening of February 2 and continued into the afternoon hours February 3. The Cooperative Observer in Rolla reported a total of 7.4 inches of sleet and snow. A glaze to as much as a tenth of an inch of ice accumulation was reported. Roads quickly became ice and snow covered and slippery. Schools were closed from February 2 to February 4.

There were 3 rounds of wintry precipitation that fell across the county. Rain changed to a mix of freezing rain sleet and snow during the early morning hours of February 2, then changed to all snow before ending around midday. The ASOS at the Springfield Branson National Airport reported 0.11 inches of flat ice accumulation with this round of precipitation. There was a lull in the action before another round of just snow began during the evening hours of February 2 and continued into the afternoon hours of February 3. The NWS office reported a total of 7.6 inches of snow with this round. The final round of snow dropped another 1.7 inches during the late evening of February 3 into the afternoon of February 4. Storm total snow was 9.5 inches measured at the NWS office. Schools were closed across the county through the entire period. Numerous accidents were reported beginning the morning of February 2 as roads became ice and snow covered and hazardous.

There were 3 rounds of wintry precipitation that fell across the county. Rain changed to freezing rain during the morning hours of February 2. Widespread reports of around 0.10 inch of ice accumulation were received. There was a lull in the action before the second round of snow began to fall during the late evening hours of February 2 and continued into February 3.  Snow was heavy at times with the Cooperative Observer at the Branson Airport reporting 6.0 inches of snowfall. After another lull in the snow, another round began shortly after midnight on February 4 and ended at the beginning of the morning commute. This round brought another 3.0 inches of snowfall as reported by the Cooperative Observer at the Branson Airport, for a storm total of 9 inches. Other locations reported 8  to 9 inches around the county. Roads became ice covered and hazardous with numerous slide offs and accidents being reported. Schools were closed through the entire period.

Drought conditions worsened over the region from early July to late July. By the last week of July, the US Drought Monitor had designated over half of the Ozarks area as being in extreme (D3) drought, Including Barry County. The rainfall received during the last week of the month eased drought conditions mainly over northern and eastern portions of the Ozarks with improvements shown in the early August Drought Monitor. Impacts across the region were primarily felt in larger scale agriculture. Farm and stock ponds saw some impacts but ground water levels and reservoirs showed little impacts. Monetary losses will be included in future reported when the drought ends and loses are assessed.

Drought conditions improved across Dallas County by the end of August. The US Drought Monitor indicated that Abnormally dry (D0) conditions remained after several rainfall events helped ease drought conditions. Impacts across the region were primarily felt in larger scale agriculture with farm and stock ponds low but improved. Much of the losses from row crops will not be felt until the fall when harvest occurs.

A rain and snow mix quickly changed over to snow during the evening hours of November 14th. Widespread snowfall ranging from 1 to 1.5 inches fell across the county. The highest amount of 1.5 inches was reported 1 mile southeast of Old Linn Creek by amateur radio. Roads became snow covered and slippery in the county during the bouts of higher snowfall rates, with several slide offs reported on Highway 42 entering Kaiser and Osage Beach.

A rain and snow mix quickly changed over to snow during the evening hours of November 14th. Widespread snowfall ranging from 2 to around 3 inches fell across the county. The highest amount of 3.2 inches was reported 3.2 miles south southeast of Stover by the CoCoRaHS observing station MO-MG-6. Roads became snow covered and slippery in the county during the bouts of higher snowfall rates.

A rain and snow mix quickly changed over to snow during the evening hours of November 14th. Widespread snowfall ranging from 2 to around 4 inches fell across the county. The highest amount of 4.2 inches was reported in Iberia by COOP observer IBEM7. A public report of 3.5 inches was reported 5 miles south southeast of Eldon. Roads became snow covered and slippery in the county during the bouts of higher snowfall rates, with multiple slide offs reported on Highway 42 just west of Highway 134. MODOT also made multiple passes with snow plows on the roads through that area.

A rain and snow mix quickly changed over to snow during the evening hours of November 14th. Widespread snowfall ranging from 1 to 2.5 inches fell across the county. The highest amount of 2.5 inches was reported 3.7 miles west northwest of Rolla by the CoCoRaHS observing station MO-PH-53. The Rolla COOP observer RRGM7 also reported 2.1 inches of snowfall. Roads became snow covered and slippery in the county during the bouts of higher snowfall rates, but had no road impacts shortly after the snowfall ended due to above freezing road and air temperatures.

Two rounds of wintry precipitation fell across the county. The first round began during the very early morning hours of January 29th as freezing drizzle and lingered into the early morning of January 30th. The second round fell during the mid morning through afternoon of January 30th and was mainly sleet mixed with some light snow. A CoCoRaHS report 1 mile southeast of Republic measured 0.4 inches of sleet and snow accumulation, mainly in the form of sleet. The NWS Springfield observation reported 0.33 inches of flat ice accretion from the 28 hours of freezing drizzle and 0.3 inches of sleet. Roads became covered and slick with numerous schools closed on January 30th and January 31st. Multiple crashes and slide offs occurred across the county, mainly occurring prior to the second round of precipitation. 17 separate crashes were reported across the county, involving 17 total vehicles and 10 total injuries.

Some schools had early release on January 24th, with numerous schools closed on January 25th and January 26th.

Rainfall through the month provided some limited help for mainly the northeastern half of the county. However, drought conditions continued across the region through the month of February. The US Drought Monitor indicated the far southwestern portion of the county as remaining in Severe (D2) Drought with the remainder of county in Moderate (D1) Drought or Abnormally Dry (D0). Impacts across the region were primarily felt in larger scale agriculture. Farm and stock ponds saw some continuing impacts with ground water levels and reservoirs showing slight drought condition improvement. Monetary crop losses for 2023 beginning January first will be included in future reports when the drought ends and loses are assessed.

Rainfall through the month provided only limited help for mainly the northern half of the county. However, drought conditions deepened across the region through the month of March. The US Drought Monitor indicated the far southern portion of the county as remaining in Severe (D2) Drought with all but the far northeastern portion of the county in Moderate (D1) Drought or Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions. Impacts across the region were primarily felt in larger scale agriculture. Farm and stock ponds saw continuing impacts with ground water levels and reservoirs showing limited drought condition improvement. Early spring crop and vegetation growth was showing signs of stress due to limited moisture. Monetary crop losses for 2023 beginning January first will be included in future reports when the drought ends and loses are assessed.

A National Weather Service storms survey determined that an EF-2 tornado with maximum winds of 122 mph touched down west of Vichy and traveled 6.8 miles lifting just northeast of the Vichy/Rolla airport. The path of the tornado was intermittent with mostly EF-1 damage but EF-2 damage did occur west of Vichy to north east of Vichy.  Along the path, which was 880 yards at its widest, multiple trees were uprooted or snapped. A home suffered significant damage to exterior walls and some interior walls. Several other homes suffered minor siding damage. Two metal frame buildings lost roofs, and another metal building had two walls blown down at the Vichy/Rolla Airport where the ASOS measured 97 mph winds. Several outbuildings suffered minor to major damage, two aircraft suffered minor damage. Five people suffered minor injuries.

A National Weather Service storm survey determined that an intermittent EF-0 tornado touched down near Fair Grove, Missouri and tracked to the northwest about a mile and a half. Maximum wind speeds were 77 mph with a maximum path width of 75 yards. Just before lifting, several outbuildings suffered significant damage.

Specific locations that flooded included the intersection of Terrell Road and Beal Road, a section of Nicholas Road just south of its intersection with Highway AA, and a low water crossing along Center Road at its intersection with Bull Creek.

Widespread flooding occurred across Vernon County as one to three inches fell over a short time duration.  The heaviest amounts fell over rural eastern Vernon County causing several sections of Highway 54 to become impassable to motorists from Nevada to Eldorado Springs.  Other locations that flooded included a section of Highway 71 north of Nevada, a section of Highway M three miles east of Horton, several sections of Highway HH, a section of Highway AA, a section of Highway M 5 miles north northwest of Walker, and a section of Highway BB three miles south of Nevada.

One to two inches of rain fell within a short time duration causing flash flooding in a few locations within Barton County.  Locations that experienced this flooding included a section of Highway 160 approximately six miles southeast of Liberal, a section of Highway 126 south of Lamar, and a section of Highway K.

Two to four inches of rain fell over Douglas County.  Widespread flash flooding occurred within low lying roads and numerous low water crossings.  A few locations that experienced flooding included city streets in the community of Ava, a section of Highway Y west of Ava, a section of Highway FF east of its intersection with Highway 14, numerous sections of Highway U, a section of Highway EE, and a section of Highway 95 near the Ozark County border.
Widespread flooding occurred across much of Polk County.  A water rescue was performed along Highway 83 in the northern section of the county.

Five inches of rain near Pleasant Hope caused the Pomme De Terre River to flood low lying areas of rural southeast Polk County.  Other low water crossings across southern Polk County also became impassable to motorists.
Flooding occurred along low lying areas near the Pomme De Terre River.

Fourty water rescues resulted from major flash flooding across Stone County.  30 people were rescued from an RV campground near Galena, while nine others were rescued from a mobile home park in Reeds Spring.  Numerous county roads were washed out with heavy damage.  A shelter was opened for flood victims.  Rainfall amounts ranged from four to seven inches.
Numerous secondary roads across the county were flooded from excessive rainfall.

A section of Highway 32 near Stockton was flooded and impassable to motorists due to excessive rainfall.  Numerous gravel roads across the county also flooded, while low water crossings became impassable to motorists.

Widespread flooding of roads and low water crossings occurred across Christian County.  Rainfall amounts ranged from two to five inches, with the heavier amounts occurring across southern Christian County.  A few locations that flooded included a section of Highway O two miles southwest of Highlandville, a low water crossing at the intersection of Bull Creek and Center Road, and section of Highway O five miles southwest of Highlandville.

Major flash flooding resulted from five to seven inches of rain that fell across Taney County.  Flash flooding occurred on Branson city roads, across railroad tracks owned by the Branson Scenic Railroad, numerous low lying roads, and almost all low water crossings.  Ten to 20 homes were damaged from flooding within the city of Branson.  Boat docks on Lake Taneycomo broke loose due to high lake levels.
Flash flooding occurred at the intersection of Highway YY and Big Bass Bend Road.  Several other low lying roads also flooded across rural eastern Barry County.

One to three inches of rain fell over Webster County.  Flooding of numerous low lying roads and low water crossings resulted.  Locations that flooded included city streets in Rogersville, city streets in Marshfield, roads in the Northview area, a section of Highway OO, a section of Bell Ford Road north of the James River, a section of Panther Creek Road north of Fordland, a section of Highway J west of Pomme De Terre Creek, a section of Interstate 44 at mile marker 91, a section of Highway B one mile south of Northview, the intersection of Highway FF and Panther Creek, a section of Highway Z south of Highway 60, a section of Ridge Road, a section of Jarrett Branch Road east of Cedar Ridge Road, and a section of Mill Dam Road near its intersection of Heritage Road.
Excessive rain caused major flash flooding at the intersection of Highway H and Highway CC in northern Greene County.
A section of Highway 95 was flooded and impassable to motorists.
Several roads north of Highway AA were flooded in the southern portion of Dallas County.

The tornado lifted 7 miles southwest of Houston in Texas County.

This storm in Howell County severely damaged three homes and completely destroyed a manufactured home, damaged several businesses, and multiple outbuildings were also heavily damaged or destroyed before moving into Shannon County.

A NWS storm survey concluded that an EF-1 tornado occurred in far southeast Oregon County to the east of Myrtle. Two homes suffered siding damage, five barns/outbuildings were destroyed, along with numerous trees suffering damage that ranged from limb damage to being uprooted along County Road 288 before the tornado crossed the Eleven Point River near the Myrtle Access and crossed into Ripley County north of County Road 286. One injury was reported. Damage cost estimates only include the Oregon County portion of the tornado track.

Route P at Big Creek was closed due to flooding. Additional county property damages were reported throughout the entire county, primarily to dirt roads and bridges, with many facilities, campgrounds, and river access points sustained damage to the Scenic Riverway parks. Damage cost estimates are a reflection of the county as a whole.  Unprecedented river levels caused devastating impacts to facilities at Akers and Pulltite. The Akers Ranger Station, which also houses Akers Ferry Canoe Rental, had approximately two feet of water throughout. The old Akers Ferry Canoe Rental store was almost fully submerged, sustaining significant damage.| |At Pulltite Campground, water reached the roof of the Pulltite Ranger Station and adjoining shower house, causing tremendous destruction. Approximately two feet of water entered the Current River Canoe Rental Store. The Pulltite picnic pavilion was swept away and destroyed. The campground amphitheater was toppled off its foundation. Floodwater lifted thick chunks of asphalt from the campground roads, undercut the roadway in multiple places, scoured campsites, and mangled or relocated posts, picnic tables, fire rings, and other structures. Large trees were toppled throughout the area and tangled with flood debris. ||Additionally, Park Rangers carried out several river rescues on Monday and Tuesday for visitors caught off guard.

Highway Y at Cowskin Creek was closed due to flooding. Additional county property damages were reported throughout the entire county, primarily to dirt roads and bridges. Damage cost estimates are a reflection of the county as a whole.

A NWS storm survey confirmed that a brief EF-0 tornado with peak winds of 77 mph, a path length of 1.40 miles, and a width of 50 yards occurred 1 mile west-northwest of Elsey in Stone County. This tornado uplifted roofs to an outbuilding and outbuilding sheds, caused roof damage to both a church and a home, and snapped several large tree branches.

Trained spotters reported the intersection of Washington Avenue and Broadway Street in West Plains was impassable due to flash flooding. Additional county property damages were reported throughout the entire county, primarily to dirt roads and bridges. Damage cost estimates are a reflection of the county as a whole.
Emergency Manager reported that a water rescue was performed off of County Road 9100 near Spring Creek.
Emergency Management reported that a water rescue was performed on County Road 1280 due to a flooded out car.
The Fire Department conducted a water rescue on Highway 17 between Roby and Success. The road was under construction, and developed large pot holes due to the flood waters washing away the roadway.
The bridge at Dogs Bluff Access on Highway 17 was reported flooded. The fire department said water has never overtopped this bridge before.
A successful water rescue occurred at a low water crossing on county road 432 in Maries County at the Bourbeuse River. A vehicle attempting to cross the river was swept off the bridge.
State Highway AB was closed due to flooding at Wolf Creek. The time of the road closure was estimated via the department of transportation traveler map.

A National Weather Service storm survey determined that an EF-0 tornado occurred near the town of Zora. Several trees were damaged along with an outbuilding. The tornado traveled along a 1.7 mile path with maximum estimated winds at 80 mph and a path width of 75 yards.
A school bus got stuck in flood waters on County Road 557 at the Stewart Creek bridge. Two students had to be rescued from the school bus.
State Highway U was closed due to excessive rainfall at Pedelo Creek.
State Highway Y was closed due to excessive rainfall at Cowskin Creek.
State Highway 95 was closed due to flooding at Bryant Creek.
State Highway U was closed due to flooding at Bryant Creek.
Highway 142 was closed due to flooding at Bennet's River.
Highway 181 was closed due to flooding at Bryant Creek.
State Highway BB was closed due to flooding of the Big Piney River.
State Highway E was closed due to flooding at the Gasconade River.
State Highway H was closed due to flooding at Spring Creek.

State Highway Z was closed due to flooding at the Finley River. A water rescue occurred at  this location due to a vehicle being swept off in flood waters. Two occupants of the vehicle were successfully rescued.

A vehicle driving on Highway H two miles east of Manes in Wright County was swept off the road into flood waters at Beaver Creek. The two occupants, ages 70 and 73 attempted to swim to dry ground and reportedly drowned.

At an unknown time on November 7th, a vehicle driving near Riddle Bridge Access along the Gasconade River in Pulaski County became submerged in the flood waters. After a search was conducted, both occupants reportedly drowned.

Dent County suffered $15M in damages, with $8M to infrastructure at Montauk State Park, along with two homes destroyed, five having major damage and another 20 with minor damage.  An additional $7M occurred to roads and bridges along with some homes.  Heaviest damages were along the Current River near Montauk State Park, Spring Creek near Salem, and Crooked Creek and Meramec River near Sligo.

The Roubidoux River flooded the Roubidoux Park and RV Park along with nearby homes. Additional damage occurred to roads and bridges across northern Pulaski County along the Roubidoux and Gasconade Rivers. Additionally, $1 million in damages occurred to road and bridge damages across the county with the most significant damage in the southern part of the county along the Little Piney and Big Piney near Devil���s Elbow. Seven homes suffered major damage and 30 homes with minor damage.
County property damages were reported throughout the entire county, primarily to dirt roads and bridges. Damage cost estimates are a reflection of the county as a whole.

Of the $1 million in damages to roads and bridges across the county, the worst damages were located along the Big Piney near Buelah, followed by the Newburg and Duke areas. Additionally, four homes suffered major damages.

The Current River reached Moderate to Major flood stage, with extensive damage reported at both Current River State Park and Echo Bluff State Park. Damage cost estimates are reflective of both State Parks.
A NWS storm survey noted small limbs down in association with a tornado.
An NWS storm survey determined a weak tornado downed small limbs.
An NWS storm survey determined that a brief tornado downed small limbs.

Video received via social media indicated a tornado touched down over the Linn Creek Cove near the Lake of the Ozarks mile marker 31.  The location of the touch down and lift is estimated.   No damage occurred so the intensity was listed as FU.

A period of significant rains fell across the region early in the month with 3 to 5 inches of rainfall measured at some locations. This allowed for drought improvements to Abnormally Dry (D0) drought by the end of the month despite little or no rain fall through the last three weeks of the month. Impacts across the region occurred over larger scale agriculture which began during the summer when Moderate (D1) drought deteriorated to Extreme (D3) drought during the month of October. Farm and stock ponds saw impacts with ground water levels also falling. Crop and vegetation growth showed signs of stress due to limited moisture with some impacts to crop yield during the fall harvest. Crop loss estimates notated are for fall harvest loses from the summer into the fall.

Firefighters in Rogersville area responded to several grass fires one of which burned in excess of 300 acers of mainly grass but which also reached some trees.
A 3185 acre wild fire, called the basin fire, occurred in the Mark Twain National Forest in eastern Taney County. The US Forest Service battled the fire and ultimately contained it.

A Red Flag Warning was in effect on March 18th. A 397 acre wildfire occurred in eastern Taney County in the Mark Twain National Forest. The US Forest Service battled the fire and ultimately contained it.

A 2100 acre wild fire occurred in southern Douglas County near State Highway N southeast of Squires, MO. Firefighters from multiple departments, the Missouri Department of Conservation and the US Forest Service worked for several days to contain the fire. The fire destroyed a shed.
A 497 acre wild fire occurred in southern Hickory County near Preston, MO. Firefighters from multiple departments battled the fire and and ultimately contained it.
A 1115 acre wildfire occurred in eastern Dallas County near Plad, MO. Firefighters battled the fire and ultimately contained it. One outbuilding was destroyed by the fire.
Several wildfires occurred across Camden County on March 18th. A total of 1900 acres burned across the western and southern portions of the county.
A 900 acre wildfire occurred in southeastern Douglas County south of Gentryville. A separate 404 acre wildfire also occurred near the town of Evans.
A 1415 acre wildfire occurred in western Shannon County near Summersville, Missouri.
A 510 acre wildfire occurred in Shannon County near Winona, MO. The fire started by a downed powerline due to high winds. The fire spread rapidly and threatened several homes.

Numerous wildfires occurred during the afternoon hours of March 14th. The majority of the fires were in southwestern Camden County just east of Macks Creek where at least 3000 acres burned. US Highway 54 had to be closed for a period of time due to low visibility from fires. Several structures were damaged or destroyed including homes, outbuildings and vehicles. The fires were eventually put out by the evening time as thunderstorms moved through the area.
A total of 993 acres burned as a result of a wildfire in Ozark county near Gainesville. The fire originally started on March 14th however it reignited a few days later.

A 793 acre wildfire burned in Dent County near Salem. The fire started on March 14th and burned for several days. Local fire departments and the Missouri Department of Conservation were able to get the fire out on March 18th.

A 450 acre wildfire burned for several days in southern Benton County near Fristoe in the Granny's Acres Conservation Area. Local fire departments and the Missouri Department of Conservation worked for several days to put out the fire.
A 576 acre wildfire occurred in Pulaski County near Crocker. This fire spread north into Miller County and was worked by several fire departments.

A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-0 tornado touched down on the far western end of Table Rock Lake, and tracked into the community of Chain of Lakes.  The tornado damaged several trees and removed shingles off of a frame house near Lake View Road.

Four to six inches of rain gradually fell over Morgan County.  A few low areas flooded including a low water crossing at the intersection of Highway AA and Cornet Creek, numerous low water crossings near Versailles, and a section of Highway BB southeast of Florence.

Four to six inches of rain gradually fell over Barry County.  A few locations flooded including a section of Farm Road 1230 southwest of Shell Knob, a section of Highway Y at its intersection with Flat Creek, a section of Highway C at its intersection with Flat Creek, and a section of Highway U at its intersection with Flatt Creek.
Six inches of rain that fell in northwest Miller County caused Blue Spring Creek to flood a section of Highway Z.

A couple of locations in eastern Greene County flooded from rainfall amounts ranging from three to five inches.  These locations that flooded were the intersection of Farm Road 172 and Farm Road 193, and the intersection of Farm 36 and Farm Road 9.

A few locations within Pulaski County flooded from rainfall amounts that ranged from four to six inches.  These locations included a section of Highway O at its intersection with Jones Creek, a section of Canyon Road at its intersection with Mill Creek, and a section of Highway O southwest of Dixon.

Three to six inches of rain fell over Maries County.  Numerous low water crossings across the county flooded.  A section of County Road 511 at its intersection with Clifty Creek had three feet of fast moving water over the road.
Five to six inches of rain fell over Phelps County.  Numerous low water crossings flooded throughout the county.
Four to five inches of rain fell over Wright County.  A section of Highway Z became flooded and impassable to motorists.
Cobb Creek flooded a section of Highway B.
A section of Highway P was closed by the Department of Transportation due to flooding.
The North Fork of the White River flooded a section of Highway EE.
A section of Highway H flooded and became impassable to motorists at its intersection with Murphy Creek.
Numerous city streets in Rolla experienced flash flooding from a training cluster of thunderstorms.  A section of Highway BB near St. James also experienced flash flooding.

An EF1 tornado with maximum wind speeds of 100 mph started 5 miles north of Seymour and tracked northeast into Wright County.  In Webster County the tornado ripped the roof off of a home, destroyed numerous barns, collapsed a train communication tower, and snapped trees.

An EF1 tornado with peak winds around 90 mph started just west of Lynchburg and tracked northeast into far northwestern Texas County. In Laclede County, the tornado damaged numerous barns and  damaged the roof of a home. Numerous trees were uprooted and damaged. The tornado then tracked northeast into Texas County.

An EF1 tornado with peak winds around 90 mph continued from Wright County into far northwestern Texas County north of Plato. In Texas County, the tornado uprooted numerous tree. The tornado then tracked northeast into Pulaski County.

An EF1 tornado with peak winds around 90 mph continued from Texas County into southern Pulaski County, including Fort Leonard Wood. In Pulaski County, the tornado damaged outbuildings and uprooted numerous trees.

Following a review of satellite and radar imagery, the NWS determined an EF-1 tornado touched down in Phelps County. This tornado was within a larger path of the parent storm that produced additional tornadoes between Diggins, MO through Rolla. This tornado started six miles west of Yancy Milles, MO in the vicinity of County Road 7630 and then tracked through the Mark Twain National Forest before lifting just before Highway 63, three miles north of Vida, MO. Based upon satellite imagery in conjunction to radar data, the endpoint of this tornado was just to the southeast of a subsequent tornado that tracked northeast toward Rolla, MO. Damage was largely to uprooted trees, though a barn damaged on Highway T near the intersection of County Road 7460.

An EF-2 tornado moved through Phelps County, including the city of Rolla.  The tornado started in the Mark Twain National Forest approximately 7 miles southeast of Newburg, MO with damage diminishing to the north of Dillion, MO. The tornado caused an intermittent path of damaged and uprooted trees before causing damage to homes and businesses along Highway 63 south of Rolla then continued to cause damage across southeast sections of Rolla that included significant damage to some homes, roof damage to multiple schools and other businesses. One person was injured across this portion of the path. The damage became more intermittent across eastern sections of Rolla, then became even more sparse as it crossed Interstate 44 at Highway V though still strong enough to damage a barn roof, uproot additional trees, and shifted a mobile home off it���s piers, and then lifted near Little Prairie Conservation Area to the north of Dillion, MO. At it���s peak, the tornado reached 500 yards wide and had peak winds estimated at 110-120 mph.

This is the continued path of the tornado that came out of Baxter County Arkansas.  An EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 145 mph moved through Bakersfield, Missouri resulting in three fatalities and four injuries. In Ozark County, the tornado destroyed several homes and damaged dozens of other homes. Multiple cars were rolled 50 to 100 yards. Numerous trees were also uprooted including entire groves of trees destroyed. This tornado then moved northeast into Howell County.

This is a continuation of the EF-3 tornado from Ozark County. This tornado traveled into southwest Howell County and continued to the northeast and passed just south of South Fork before causing damage along the portion of Highway 63 that turns southeast as it exits West Plains. The tornado finally lifted along Highway 160 seven miles east of West Plains. In Howell County, the tornado damaged numerous homes and uprooted numerous trees.

This is the beginning of a long-track EF-3 tornado that began south of Rover, MO and tracked northeast before lifting in southern Reynolds County. The peak wind speed was 165 mph with a maximum width of 800 yards. The tornado initially touched down around 2 miles northeast of Brandsville, then moved south of Rover where it pushed two homes off their foundation before continuing northeast through wooded areas. The tornado then took the roof off another home but left internal walls intact along Highway DD and again at the north end of County Road 331. It was also at this point that it caused the collapse of a pair of new high voltage transmission line metal support polls rated to withstand 90 mph winds before going back into wooded areas where satellite imagery depicted periodic uprooted trees into the Mark Twain National Forest. Thousands of trees were uprooted along its path. The tornado then traveled northeast into Shannon and eventually Carter Counties.

This is the continuation of the tornado out of Oregon County that moved into far southeastern Shannon County. This tornado uprooted hundreds of trees before moving northeast into Carter County and intensifying.

A 24 mile long tornado path was determined by a combination of NWS survey, storm reports, and satellite damage to have moved from just north of Koshkonong to 2 miles north of Alton before lifting 8 miles northeast of Alton. Maximum width was approximately a half mile wide though it was likely considerably narrower in places. While much of the path was to trees along with several outbuildings, the tornado damaged a few homes including a south facing ground level home off County Road 402 where it caused EF3 damage. The track continued northeast of Alton into the Mark Twain National Forest with satellite detecting an intermittent path of uprooted trees to near the Eleven Point River at Turners Mill.

A National Weather Service Storm survey determined that an EF-1 tornado touched down north of Bronaugh and tracked northeast on a route just east of a separate tornado that tracked through the Moundville area. Based upon radar, satellite imagery and ground surveys, the Bronaugh tornado caught up to the initial tornado then continued through Nevada and lifted west of Walker. In it���s early stages, two separate tornado debris signatures were detected by the KSGF 88D radar. Initially causing damage only to trees and barns, the tornado damaged several homes and outbuildings as it tracked toward Nevada, damaged numerous businesses as it crossed Highway 54 at Nevada. The tornado knocked over two sets of four railroad cars sitting on a side rail to the northeast of Nevada yet nearby trees only suffering limb damage. The tornado continued to damage outbuildings and barns as it tracked across open farmland before lifting near Walker.

A National Weather Service survey found a brief EF-0 tornado touched down in far southeastern Greene County. Damage included broken branches and damage to a few outbuildings. Sheet metal and debris were displaced to the east in a field near the intersection of East Farm Road 186 and South Farm Road 203. Maximum wind speeds of 70 mph.

An EF-0 tornado touched down in south-central Barton County in Missouri at 2:29 PM on April 20, 2025, tracking northeast through the city of Lamar before finally lifting northeast of Milford at 2:50 PM. The majority of damage from this tornado was in the city of Lamar, where it caused light to moderate damage to around 200 homes and businesses. Eyewitness accounts report a rain-wrapped tornado, and much of the debris field left behind consisted of light debris like leaf litter pressed to multiple sides of impacted structures by the rain. Straight line wind damage was also found to the east of the path in Lamar.

A National Weather Service survey indicated that at 4:59 PM on April 20, 2025, an EF-0 tornado touched down just west of Highway 5 in Wright County, about 5 miles south of Hartville. The tornado traveled northeast and crossed the highway before lifting at Wolf Creek at 5:01 PM. This tornado damaged numerous trees and uprooted a few others. One of the tree limbs fell on a house, which caused significant roof damage.

A National Weather Service survey found that an EF-0 A tornado touched down south of Mill Creek in Morgan County, Missouri at 4:30 PM on April 20, 2025. This tornado removed multiple turkey/chicken barn roof panels, in addition to breaking several large tree limbs. The tornado lifted at 4:32 PM.

A National Weather Service Survey determined that an EF0 tornado developed at 4:46PM April 20, 2025 northwest of High Prairie, MO and tracked to the northeast for a little over one mile lifting at 4:48pm. Peak winds were 80mph with a max width of 30 yards. Several barns were damaged along with several trees and limbs downed along the path.

An NWS storm survey and public drone video determined an EF-1 with 80-90 mph winds uprooted numerous trees starting near the intersection of Highway 38 and Highway E to the east of Hartville...then intermittently across fields south of Highway 38 and before crossing the Highway to the north of Latham Mill and then into the Dove Creek basin. It is unknown whether the path continued further into a wooded area west of Rayborn. Trees showed a convergent fall pattern as the tornado crossed the highway and through creek. Maximum winds were 90 mph and the width was 400 yards with 80-90 mph winds uprooted numerous trees starting near the intersection of Highway 38 and Highway E to the east of Hartville...then intermittently across fields south of Highway 38 and before crossing the Highway to the north of Latham Mill and then|into the Dove Creek basin. It is unknown whether the path continued further into a wooded area west of Rayborn. Trees showed a convergent fall pattern as the tornado crossed the highway and through the creek basin. Maximum winds were 90 mph and the width was 400 yards.
A short-lived EF0 tornado downed large limbs and caused minor shingle and siding damage to a home before the path was no longer visible into a forested area.
An EF0 tornado damaged trees, including some being uprooted in a cyclonic pattern along an intermittent path between Highway O and Highway 14. A few homes and cars were damaged by falling limbs.

An EF-1 tornado that touched down 3 miles southwest of Galena tracked into Missouri  at the intersection of SE Turkey Creek Road and North State Line Avenue. The tornado continued northeast through Carl Junction before lifting near the intersection of County Road 320 and H Highway in northern Jasper County. Multiple witnesses reported the tornado to be rain-wrapped as it impacted dozens of trees, with damage ranging from large limbs down to others being uprooted.  Wind speeds associated with the uprooted trees were reduced as damages to nearby structures were largely limited to shingles and siding, and very wet grounds being a contributing factor.

A National Weather Service storm survey determined that a brief, weak EF-0 tornado began at 9:30 AM near Eaglecrest St. The tornado damaged an auto repair shop with partial roof removal and wall collapse. The tornado path was intermittent to the northeast crossing Highway 160 before lifting near a storage shed business where awning damage occurred and a travel trailer was overturned.

An National Weather Service survey found that an EF-1 tornado began at 9:00 AM near Highway 60 between Verona and Aurora and ended in eastern Aurora just east of Highway 60. The tornado had a path length of 4.88 miles, a width of 100 yards, and maximum wind speeds of 90 mph. The tornado damaged the roof of a church, caused minor damage to several other structures, and uprooted many large trees.

An NWS survey found that an EF-1 tornado began at 8:55 AM 3 miles south of Freistatt near CR 1090 and CR 2210. The tornado had a path length of 4.18 miles, a width of 100 yards, and maximum wind speeds of 90 mph. It ended at 9:00 AM around CR 1125 and CR 1131. The tornado uprooted many trees and damaged many large limbs. It also damaged the roofs of outbuildings including a turkey barn and a residence. At its peak intensity, the tornado destroyed a small outbuilding, uprooted many trees, downed powerlines, and threw tin well downwind.

A National Weather Service survey found that an EF-0 tornado began at 9:09 AM near the Lawrence County and Stone County line along CR 2210, about 2 miles west of Bradfield. The tornado had a path length of 5.17 miles, a width of 50 yards, and maximum wind speeds of 80 mph. It ended at 9:14 AM along Barke Road on the Lawrence County border side of the intersection of Stone and Christian counties.  The tornado mainly uprooted many large trees in a convergent pattern, resulting in some nearby structural damage to a few outbuildings.

A National Weather Service survey determined that an EF0 tornado began at 8:35 am near Boulder City and moved nearly due north for around 2 miles with a maximum width of 50 yards and peak winds of 80 mph. Along its path the weak tornado damaged numerous trees with some uprooted. A couple outbuildings also suffered minor damage as well.

A National Weather Service storm survey determined that an EF-0 tornado touched down west of Fair Grove around 9:40 AM and lifted around 10:10 east of Bassville, MO. Many trees were uprooted or split and many large limbs broken. A small residence and farm outbuilding sustained minor damage. Damage was limited along the western portion of the track and was observed to increase along and east of Farm Roads 181 and 48. Before diminishing again as it approached Highway 65, with greater tree damage again viewed east of the Highway before the path ended east of Bassville.

Five to six inches of rain fell over Bourbon County.  This excessive rain caused widepsread flooding of numerous small streams, creeks, and two main stem rivers.  A few specific locations that flooded include a section of Highway 31 at its intersection with the Little Osage River, a section of County Road 1198 at its intersection with the Robinson Branch of the Marmaton River, a section of 205th Street, and a section of Poplar Road.  205th Street and Poplar Road were flooded from tributaries of Mill Creek.

Three to five inches of rain fell over Barry County resulting in widespread flooding of small streams and creeks.  Flatt Creek appeared to be impacted the greatest, flooding several low lying roads and low water crossings.  Other specific locations that experienced flooding included a section of Highway 60 near its intersection with Kyler Road, numerous streets in Monett, several streets in the city of Cassville, a section of Highway 76 near Cassville, a section of Highway 39 near its intersection with Farm Road 2135, a section of Highway C near McDowell, and a section of Highway 97 west of Monett. Five to six inches of rain fell over Stone County resulting in widespread flash flooding of small streams, creeks, and one main stem river.  The James River appeared to be impacted the greatest, as it flooded several roads and low lying areas.  The city of Reeds Springs was also impacted by flooding, as sections of the city were inundated by Railey Creek.

Five to six inches of rain fell over Christian County resulting in widespread flooding of small streams, creeks, and the Finley River.  Bull Creek appeared to be impacted the greatest, as it flooded numerous roads and low water crossings.  The Finley River was also heavily impacted as it flooded sections of Ozark.  The Finley River also closed down a section of Riverdale Road west of Ozark.

Three to five inches of rain fell over Pulaski County resulting in flooding of small streams, creeks, and two rivers.  The Gasconade and Big Piney rivers appeared to be impacted the greatest as they flooded numerous roads and low lying areas.  Low water crossings countywide were impassable to motorists.  Also, a section of Highway 133 at Fox Crossing was closed due to flooding, while numerous city streets in Dixon were flooded.  A section of Highway O at its intersection with Jones Creek was flooded.

Three to five inches of rain fell over Taney County resulting in flooding of small streams, creeks, and Lake Taneycomo.  Turkey Creek flooded the Hidden Valley Trailer Park in Hollister as numerous mobile homes were inundated.  Meanwhile, Bull Creek flooded into a housing subdivision that was in the process of being built.  Also, Lake Taneycomo flooded into some homes as levels increased in response to a water release from Table Rock Lake.

Two to five inches of rain fell over Douglas County resulting in widespread flooding of small streams and creeks.  The western section of the county experienced the greatest amount of rain, while the eastern edge of the county only experienced around two inches.  Specific locations that were flooded included a section of Highway B north of Ava, downtown Ava, a section of Highway N north of Ava, and nearly all low water crossings across much of the county.

Two to four inches of rain fell over Texas County resulting in flooding in some areas.  The Big Piney River appeared to be impacted the greatest flooding several low lying roads and low water crossings.  The city of Cabool experienced flash flooding on numerous city streets.  All of this flooding resulted in several miles of road damage along with two bridges that were washed out.
Flash flooding occurred along Pidgeon Creek which caused all campers on Montauk State Park to evacuate.

Five to six inches of rain fell over Miller County resulting in flooding of small streams and creeks.  Numerous gravel roads and all low water crossings were impassable across the county.

Three to five inches of rain fell over Maries County resulting in widespread flooding of small creeks and streams.  Numerous county roads were flooded and all low water crossings were impassable to motorists.

Four to six inches of rain fell over Webster County resulting in flooding of numerous main stem rivers, creeks, and small streams. A NWS survey team found intermittent EF-0 tornado damage with maximum winds of 85 mph northwest of Willow Springs in Howell County. Several trees along the path were uprooted and/or snapped, and a donkey barn was lifted off the ground.
A NWS survey team concluded that a brief EF-1 tornado touched down between Cabool and Simmons in Texas County, with maximum winds of 94 mph. Two barns were destroyed, with several trees uprooted.
A NWS survey team found EF-1 damage with maximum winds of 93 mph near Eunice in Texas County. Multiple trees were uprooted and/or snapped along the path, and a barn roof was damaged.
An EF-0 tornado briefly touched down approximately 4 miles north of Hartshorn in Texas County. Numerous large trees were uprooted, and a few smaller trees were snapped.

An EF-1 tornado briefly touched down approximately 5 miles southwest of Akers in Shannon County. Strong winds caused the roof of a single wide home to be torn off as well as the windows to be blown in. Other damage included large trees uprooted and healthy trees snapped.

A NWS survey team found EF-0 damage with maximum winds of 85 mph south of Summersville in Texas County that later tracked into Shannon County. Multiple trees and limbs along the path were uprooted and/or snapped. Additionally, several roofs were damaged, including a barn roof that was partially removed, a metal roof that was removed from its building and blown away, and other buildings that suffered shingle damage.

A National Weather Service storm survey determined that an EF1 Tornado with estimated wind speeds of 105 mph touched down near the northeast portion of Hallowell before tracking 4.37 miles to the east. The tornado uprooted or snapped several trees, overturned several empty railcars, caused significant damaged to several grain bins, destroyed multiple outbuildings and snapped or broke numerous power poles and downed power lines.  The tornado track ended approximately 1.25 miles east of Sherwin.

A National Weather Service survey concluded an EF1 tornado with peak winds of 95mph damaged an outdoor maintenance storage building at the golf course at the W 2nd Street and S Schifferdecker Ave in Joplin. The tornado then tracked to the northeast downing numerous trees in a cyclonic manner. Minor roof damage occurred to a few homes, and several other homes were damaged by trees falling on them.

A National Weather Service survey concluded an EF0 tornado caused damage to a building on 83 and Highway MM southeast of Warsaw. This tornado is also damaged multiple trees in the area which was confirmed via Sentinel-2 satellite data analysis. The tornado had maximum winds of 80 mph and was on the ground for about 0.4miles with a width of 200 yards.

An National Weather Service survey concluded an EF1 tornado touched down southwest of Warsaw, crossing the lake, and tracking just east of Highway 65. The tornado flipped several mobile homes resting on blocks, damaged signs and roofing associated with stores along Highway 65, and created a pattern of tree damage including many uprooted or snapped, surveyed through in-person and Sentinel-2 satellite surveys. The tornado tracked for a little over 6 miles with a path width of 200 yards and maximum wind speeds of 90mph.

A National Weather Survey determined that an EF0 tornado caused debris from a barn and outbuildings to be thrown mainly east with some north near the beginning of the tornadoes track. Numerous trees were also uprooted and damaged along with many large limbs downed along McCasland Road. The tornado tracked for about 1.25 miles with a path width of 100 yards and maximum winds of 80mph.

A combination of ground National Weather Service surveys and Sentinel-2 satellite data concluded an EF1 tornado occurred 2 miles north of Gravois Mills. Several trees were uprooted in a cyclonic pattern and multiple other trees and limbs were damaged along the tornado's path. A window on a home was broken and two outbuildings suffered damage. Along the slightly over 7 mile track of the tornado maximum winds were 90mph with a width of 300 yards.

A National Weather Service survey found damage associated with a tornado that tracked north of Barnett, MO for 1.3 miles. Damage included tree debris blown to the east and north, and metal rods sheltering hay bales bent. Winds along the tornadoes 150 yard wide path were estimated at 85mph.

A National Weather Service survey determined that an EF0 tornado with maximum winds of 70mph produced an intermittent damage path to the east northeast of Buffalo, MO. Reports of a funnel cloud near the ground were received from the Springfield Street area southeast of Buffalo, with the first damage viewed north of Quarry Road in a wooded area. The tornado did the majority of its damage as it crossed Ozark Trail. One mobile home suffered broken glass on the south and north sides of the structure and another on the east side of the structure. Additional damage was noted to several outbuildings. Additional large limbs were noted on Steelman Road and west of Engle Road via Sentinel-2 satellite data analysis.

A National Weather Service survey determined that an EF0 tornado with winds up to 80mph briefly touched down north of Pumpkin Center. Along the storms path, numerous homes, vehicles, businesses, equipment, crops, livestock and other structures were damaged by hail before the storm passed into southeastern Lawrence County.

Along the storms path, numerous homes, vehicles, businesses, equipment, crops, livestock and other structures were damaged by hail before the storm passed into southwestern Greene County.

A hail swath from a mile to 3 miles wide began southwest of Republic and continued to the northeast across Greene County. Hail from quarters to 4.75 inches in size fell along a path from Republic to northwestern Springfield to Fair Grove as an intensifying left moving supercell moved to the northeast across the County. Along the storms path, numerous homes, vehicles, businesses, equipment, crops, livestock and other structures were damaged by hail before the storm passed into northwestern Webster County.  ||As the storm moved across northwestern Springfield, it moved over the Springfield-Branson National Airport where 4 commuter jets, two cargo jets and up to 25 general aviation aircraft were on the TARMAC. Over 1200 vehicles were in the short and long term parking lot. The storm them moved over the Springfield Zoo killing an Emu and injuring another. At least two dozen people were injured by hail by being outside during the hail.

Excessive rainfall caused flooding over a few city streets in Neosho.
A few roads across Benton County became flooded and impassable to motorists.
Flash flooding occurred at the intersection of Battlefield and Scenic.
Excessive rain caused several roads across the county to flood.
Thunderstorm wind gusts damaged shingles, windows, and trees in the Carl Junction area.
Thunderstorm wind gusts caused roof damage to a school.
Thunderstorm wind gusts downed several trees.

Excessive rainfall caused several roads and low water crossings to become flooded across the county.  A couple of specific locations that flooded included the intersection of 165th street and Highway 31, along with the intersection of 185th Street and Highway 31.
Law enforcement determined that lightning struck a brick mailbox causing bricks to scatter.  One brick was thrown though a window of a house while a couple of vehicles were damaged.
Baseball size hail damaged windows of a house near Stoutland.

A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-0 tornado touched down along the northwestern edge of Nixa and tracked to near Highway 160 between Tracker Road and Highway CC.  Wind speeds were estimated at 80 mph which damaged more than a dozen homes.
Severe thunderstorm wind gusts downed several trees near the intersection of Business 71 and Sugar Creek.
Thunderstorm wind gusts blew a roof off of a structure along Highway 59.
Thunderstorm wind gusts knocked over trees and power lines.
A few trees were knocked down from thunderstorm wind gusts.
Thunderstorm wind gusts knocked over a power pole near the intersection of Battlefield and Scenic.
Thunderstorm wind gusts knocked over trees and power lines along Tracker Road.
Severe thunderstorm wind gusts knocked over a section of a building.
An outbuilding sustained damage from severe thunderstorm wind gusts.
Severe thunderstorm wind gusts destroyed a barn and damaged numerous trees near the intersection of Buckbrush Road and Harmony Road.
A few power poles were damaged from severe thunderstorm wind gusts.
Thunderstorm wind gusts damaged the roof of a church and knocked over a few trees.
Severe thunderstorm wind gusts destroyed a barn.
Excessive rain caused sections of Highway 37 and Highway 90 near Seligman to experience flash flooding.
A section of Highway 59 was flooded from Butler Creek rising out of its banks.
Excessive rain caused flooding across a section of Forest Avenue.
Several buildings were damaged near the intersection of Highway 76 and Highway 59.

Several roads and low water crossings across the county became flooded and impassable to motorists.  Three specific locations that flooded include a section of Highway U, a section of Highway Y, and a section of Highway 76.

Several areas of Bourbon County flooded as three to four inches of rain fell during the morning hours.  A few specific locations that flooded include a section of County Road 195 near its intersection with Highway 31, a section of County Road 165 west of Fulton, a low water crossing near the intersection of County Road 205 and Poplar Road, the intersection of County Road 65 and Yale Road, and the intersection of County Road 85 and Maple.
A section of Highway WW was flooded at its intersection with Big Buffalo Creek.
The Little Osage River flooded a section of Highway V north of Stotesbury.
Flooding occurred along a few creeks in northwest Benton County.  One fatality occurred when a rancher was checking on his cattle and was swept into a flooded creek.
The Neosho River flooded a large section of western Cherokee County.  Fly Creek also flooded several roads in southwest sections of the county.
Heavy rain caused six low water crossings across the county to become flooded.

The Republic Emergency Management Director visually spotted and tracked a tornado that touched down southwest of Republic and moved across the city.  Approximately 50 structures were damaged.  The heaviest damage appeared to be concentrated on Kristopher Street.

A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-1 tornado touched down in a field about one quarter of a mile west of the intersection of Willard Road and Farm Road 115.  A house located along Farm Road 115 sustained heavy damage.  A few outbuidlings at the same location were destroyed.  The tornado crossed Highway 160, and lifted approximately two miles south of Fantastic Caverns.

A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-0 tornado touched down near the intersection of Highway 13 and Highway WW.  The tornado tracked to the northeast over an intermittent path prior to lifting near the intersection of Highway H and Farm Road 148.  The tornado damaged several outbuildings and trees along its path.

A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-1 tornado touched down approximately two miles northwest of Brighton, and tracked north across southern Polk County.  The tornado lifted approximately two miles east southeast of Bolivar.  The tornado damaged or destroyed several outbuildings and barns, and caused moderate to severe damage to frame homes.  In addtion, numerous trees were uprooted.

This tornado is an extension of the Taney County tornado.  A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-1 tornado impacted extreme southeast Christian County.  Wind speeds were estimated at 100 mph as the tornado damaged two homes, destroyed a few outbuildings, and downed numerous trees.  The tornado eventually tracked into western Douglas County.

This tornado is an extension of the Christian County tornado.  A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-1 tornado tracked into southwest Douglas County.  Trees and a few outbuildings were damaged from the tornado.

A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-2 tornado with winds up to 130 mph touched down approximately one mile north of Merritt.  The tornado tracked northeast along a two and a half mile path before lifting northwest of Goodhope.  The tornado damaged two homes, several outbuildings, and numerous trees.

A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-2 tornado touched down two miles west of Goodhope and tracked northeast for about two and a half miles.  The tornado tore a roof off of a home along with damaging numerous trees.

A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-1 tornado touched down near Highway 60 approximately one mile east of Fordland, and tracked northeast to near Diggins Road.  The tornado damaged a delivery truck, a roof off the Memory Lane Dairy Farm, several trees, and an outbuilding on Diggins Road.

A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-2 tornado touched down two miles west of Charity and tracked northeast over an intermittent path.  The tornado destroyed three frame homes and numerous outbuildings.  One indirect fatality and another injury resulted from this tornado.  A man and his wife were both injured when their house was destroyed.  He later died from a heart attack while being transported to the hospital.

A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-1 tornado touched down near Mt. Zion and tracked about one mile to the northeast.  The tornado caused minor home damage, destroyed a barn, and uprooted several trees.

A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-1 tornado with 90 to 100 mph winds occurred four miles northwest of Hartville.  The tornado destroyed several outbuildings and uprooted numerous trees.
A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-2 tornado touched down near the small community of Oakland.  This tornado damaged numerous outbuildings and destroyed a mobile home.

A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-1 tornado impacted a rural section of northwest Ozark County.  The tornado destroyed seven outbuildings and damaged three houses.  Tree damage was intense, particularly near the intersection of County Road 950 and County Road 955.

A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-1 tornado impacted a section of northeast Texas County.  The tornado removed a roof from a mobile home and destroyed a barn.  Numerous trees were also uprooted.

A National Weather Service storm survey revealed that an EF-3 tornado impacted a rural area just north of Pomona.  The tornado destroyed a frame home.  Several cars were thrown 50 yards while two school buses were knocked over.  One mobile home and one travel trailer were destroyed, and two outbuildings along with an auto shop were destroyed.
